reason: The sources provide over a dozen corroborated claims across multiple independent sites detailing the station's scale, assembly, and decommissioning.
story: Orbiting 250 miles above Earth at five miles per second, the International Space Station is the largest human-made structure ever placed in space. Built through more than 40 assembly flights by an international partnership of 15 nations, the outpost spans 356 feet end-to-end—rivaling the size of an American football field and weighing over 900,000 pounds. Yet despite its massive footprint, its pressurized interior equals just a single Boeing 747 airliner. Since November 2000, the station has sustained continuous human habitation, with crews circling the globe every 90 minutes while conducting breakthrough research and testing hardware for future missions to Mars. However, this orbital giant cannot fly forever. Aging structural hulls, radiator leaks, and atmospheric drag mean its days are numbered. By 2030, NASA and its international partners plan to use a specialized deorbit spacecraft to steer the 400-plus-ton station into a targeted, destructive reentry over the remote Pacific Ocean.
angle: Spanning 356 feet from end to end—as wide as an entire football field and weighing over 900,000 pounds—the ISS has an internal pressurized volume comparable to just a single Boeing 747 airliner.

claims.claim: The International Space Station is the largest human-built structure ever constructed in space.
Construction of the ISS began in 1998 with the launch of its first module, Zarya.
The space station spans approximately 356 feet (109 meters) end-to-end, covering the area of an American football field.
The station weighs over 900,000 pounds (approximately 410,000 to 430,000 kilograms).
The station has an internal pressurized volume of approximately 1,000 to 1,005 cubic meters (around 35,000 to 35,491 cubic feet), comparable to a Boeing 747 airliner.
Assembling the station required more than 40 delivery flights.
The space station has been continuously occupied by humans since November 2000.
The ISS orbits Earth at an altitude of approximately 250 miles (400 to 410 kilometers).
The station circles Earth roughly every 90 to 93 minutes.
The station travels at an orbital velocity of approximately five miles per second (about 17,200 mph or 7.67 km/s).
The space station program is operated through an international partnership of five space agencies representing 15 countries.
A standard resident crew on the ISS consists of seven people.
The station flies in an orbital inclination of approximately 51.6 degrees.
The Russian science laboratory module Nauka launched and docked to the station in July 2021.
The ISS is planned to end operations and be deorbited around 2030.
Surviving debris from the station's final deorbit will be targeted to crash into a remote region of the Pacific Ocean.
NASA is procuring a dedicated U.S. Deorbit Vehicle (USDV) to perform the final reentry burn.
In January 2020, NASA awarded Axiom Space a contract to attach commercial modules to the ISS.
Former NASA Administrator Charles Bolden emphasized that any human mission to Mars is likely to be a global effort.

disputed: Overall structural dimensions: S1 and S2 state the Integrated Truss Structure itself is 356 feet (108.5 meters) long, whereas NASA (S3) states the truss is 310 feet (94 meters) and that 356 feet is the solar array wingspan and total end-to-end station length. Scripts should describe the 356-foot figure as the station's overall end-to-end span or wingspan rather than the truss length alone.

Exact total mass: Sources vary from approximately 410,000 kg / 900,000 lb (S2) to 925,335 lb / 419,725 kg (S3), 430 metric tons (S6), and 500 tons cited in Russian rhetoric (S1). Scripts should state 'over 900,000 pounds' or 'over 400 metric tons' rather than an exact single-digit pound figure.

Total project cost: S2 cites a cost of around $150 billion USD, while S7 refers to it as a '$100 billion orbiting lab.' Scripts should avoid a single definitive dollar figure or attribute it as 'estimated between 100 and 150 billion dollars.'
